title: Aggregate supply
competency: Define aggregate supply, explain why SRAS slopes up and LRAS is vertical, and describe what shifts SRAS.

en.text: Aggregate supply is the quantity of all goods and services (real GDP) supplied at various price levels, other things equal. In the short run the relationship is positive, so SRAS slopes up. The Keynesian AS curve is horizontal because unemployed labour lets firms supply any amount at the current price level; the classical AS curve is vertical because the labour market is always at full employment.

The labour market is always at full employment

screens.why: p.36: the long run is long enough to vary all inputs.

screens.why: Idle labour and machines can be used at the same wage and cost, so the Keynesian AS is flat: output rises, prices do not.

ideas.name: Why SRAS slopes up: sticky wages and misperceptions

en.text: Firms pay nominal wages but hire according to real wages, where real wage = nominal wage ÷ price level. If nominal wages are sticky and the price level falls, the real wage rises, so firms hire fewer workers and output falls. If workers misperceive the price level, they may think their real wage fell and supply less labour. Either way a lower price level brings lower output, so SRAS slopes up.

screens.ask: Your wage is fixed at $30 an hour by contract. Prices of everything fall. What happens to what your wage can buy?
screens.after: Your real wage rises. For the employer, each worker now costs more in real terms.

screens.title: Sticky wages
paras: Wages are often "locked in" by labour contracts for one to three years.
Or they stay fixed by social conventions and ideas of fairness.
Management knows its labour costs; workers know pay will not be cut.

screens.title: Sticky wages: a firm with 1,000 workers
steps: Contract: $30 an hour; price index expected to stay 1.50.
The firm cuts workers from 1,000 to 800.
Fewer workers → less output. Lower price level, lower output: SRAS slopes up.

screens.title: Worker misperceptions
steps: After: nominal wage $25, price index 1.25. Real wage = 25 ÷ 1.25 = $20, unchanged.
Workers wrongly think prices fell only to 1.39.

The price index falls to 1.25; the nominal wage stays $30. Real wage = $___
screens.why: 30 ÷ 1.25 = 24: $4 (20%) higher than expected.

screens.ask: A worker earns $25 and believes the price index is 1.39. Perceived real wage = $___ (2 decimal places)
screens.why: 25 ÷ 1.39 = 17.9856… ≈ $17.99 (the book truncates to $17.98). The true real wage is 25 ÷ 1.25 = $20.

screens.why: P ↓ with W fixed → W ÷ P ↑ → labour demanded ↓ → output ↓.

opts: Labour contracts lock them in for years
Firms do not know their costs
screens.ans: Labour contracts lock them in for years

screens.text: With sticky nominal wages, a rise in the price level lowers the real wage.
screens.why: Real wage = W ÷ P: a bigger P with the same W gives a smaller real wage, so firms hire more.

screens.ask: A firm pays a fixed 45 Birr an hour. The price index rises from 1.50 to 1.80. The real wage falls by ___ Birr
screens.why: 45 ÷ 1.50 = 30; 45 ÷ 1.80 = 25; fall = 5 Birr. Cheaper real labour → firms hire more → output rises with the price level.
screens.clue: Find both real wages, then subtract.

en.text: A change in the price level moves the economy along SRAS. Other factors shift the whole curve: input prices (especially wages), resource availability, imported resource prices, market power, productivity, technology, business taxes and subsidies, and weather. Profit per unit = price per unit − cost per unit: higher costs at the same price lower profit and output, shifting SRAS left; lower costs shift it right.

am.text: የዋጋ ደረጃ ለውጥ በኩርባው ላይ እንቅስቃሴ ነው። ደመወዝ፣ የግብዓት ዋጋ፣ ቴክኖሎጂ፣ ግብርና የአየር ሁኔታ SRASን ያንቀሳቅሳሉ።

screens.title: Guess: more or less output at the same price level?
screens.after: At a given price level, anything that lowers cost per unit raises output: SRAS shifts right.

screens.title: Movement or shift of SRAS?
paras: A change in the price level changes quantity supplied: a movement along SRAS.
Other factors shift the whole SRAS curve.

screens.title: Factors that shift SRAS
paras: a) Cost of inputs (change in input prices)
b) Domestic resource availability: managerial ability, land, labour, capital; price of imported resources; market power
c) Change in productivity
d) State of technology
e) Tax policy: business taxes and subsidies
f) Weather (mainly farm output)

paras: Labour is usually a firm's biggest cost.
Profit per unit = Price per unit − Cost per unit.
Higher wages at the same price → lower profit → firms produce less.
Figure 2.4: at P₁ output falls Q₁ → Q₂ (A → B): SRAS₁ shifts left to SRAS₂.
Lower wages: Q₁ → Q₃ (A → C): SRAS shifts right to SRAS₃.

steps: Price per unit 50 Birr; cost per unit 40 Birr.
Wages rise: cost per unit becomes 46 Birr; price stays 50.
Firms produce less at the same price level: SRAS shifts left.

screens.text: Wage rates rise across the economy. The SRAS curve
screens.why: Higher wages raise cost per unit, so less is supplied at every price level (Figure 2.4, A → B).

screens.title: SRAS shifts right or left?
items: The price of imported oil rises
screens.why: Lower cost per unit or more resources → right; higher cost or lost resources → left.
screens.clue: Does the change raise or lower cost per unit?

screens.ask: Price per unit 80 Birr, cost per unit 60 Birr. Costs rise to 70 Birr. Profit per unit falls from 20 to ___ Birr
screens.why: 80 − 70 = 10 Birr: half the profit, so firms supply less.

screens.text: In Figure 2.4 the price level stays at P₁, yet output changes from Q₁ to Q₃. This is
opts: a shift of SRAS to the right
screens.ans: a shift of SRAS to the right
screens.why: Output changed with no change in the price level, so the curve itself moved (lower wages).

screens.text: Which is a movement along SRAS, not a shift?
opts: The price level rises and firms supply more
screens.ans: The price level rises and firms supply more
screens.why: Only a price-level change moves along the curve.

screens.text: Ethiopian farms adopt better seeds while the price of imported fertiliser doubles. What can we say about SRAS?
opts: It may shift either way: the two changes pull in opposite directions
It cannot move, only AD moves
screens.ans: It may shift either way: the two changes pull in opposite directions
screens.why: Better seeds (technology) push SRAS right; dearer imported inputs push it left. The net shift depends on which is bigger.

en.text: SRAS slopes up only while wages are sticky or workers misperceive prices. In the long run wages become flexible and perceptions accurate, and the economy produces full-employment, or natural, real GDP (Qₙ). The LRAS curve is therefore vertical at Qₙ: the same output at every price level. Long-run equilibrium is real GDP at Qₙ with wages and prices fully adjusted.

am.text: በረጅም ጊዜ ደመወዝ ይስተካከላል፣ የተሳሳተ ግንዛቤ ይጠፋል። LRAS በተፈጥሯዊ እውነተኛ ምርት (Qₙ) ላይ ቀጥ ያለ መስመር ነው።

screens.title: After a few years
screens.ask: Contracts are renewed and workers see prices correctly. Will a higher price level still raise output?
opts: No, output returns to its full-employment level
screens.after: In the long run wages adjust and misperceptions end, so the price level no longer changes output.

screens.title: The long run
paras: SRAS slopes up because of sticky wages and misperceptions.
In time, wages become flexible and perceptions become accurate.
Then the economy is in the long run.
It produces full-employment, or natural, real GDP (Qₙ).
LRAS is a vertical line at Qₙ: the same output at every price level (Figure 2.5).

screens.title: Long-run equilibrium
paras: Wages and prices have adjusted to their final levels.
Workers have no misperceptions.
Real GDP equals natural real GDP, Qₙ.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS)
A vertical curve at natural real GDP: in the long run output does not depend on the price level.
Natural real GDP
The full-employment real GDP (Qₙ) the economy produces in the long run.
Long-run equilibrium
Real GDP when wages and prices have fully adjusted and there are no misperceptions: natural real GDP.
